**Why I’m Writing to You** 

Dearest VA, 

I first fell in love with the practice of public relations years ago as a fashion designer. Operating on a shoestring, I was pattern maker, project manager, fashion designer, CEO, and publicist of my first company. I painstakingly learned, through trial and error, that failure is part of the journey. But once I uncovered a bit of success and found publicity in major fashion media, the doors began opening… Clients heard my name and took my calls… I was hooked on publicity\! 

Fast forward a number of years now. Inspired to help other entrepreneurs and small business owners benefit from PR as I have, I left fashion and got started applying my passion and skill in public relations and marketing. I began with an ad agency, developing their prospects and marketing materials from scratch – sparking growth and igniting their bottom line. Next, I broke ground in my own strategy firm, helping entrepreneurs to launch their businesses online. Soon, I would write my own book, *Plain Jane’s Promotional Planner*. 

I often hear from my clients that they would love to benefit from PR, but they just can’t bring themselves to really invest the time and money into what public relations might or might not be able to do for them. I am a self-professed PR professional, and half-geek, so helping entrepreneurs and business owners discover what they need to take command of their PR is my domain. Of course, I began to wonder what more I could be offering my clients to help them feel confident enough to take the leap into PR. How could I help prepare  
or assist them? Then it struck me how pivotal of a role the Virtual Assistant could hold on a PR team. 

Helen Keller once said, “Alone we can do so little – together we can do so much.” Over the years I have learned that we should never try to forge it alone. Instead, we should aim to seek out support in the form of mentors and like-minded communities – courageously exploring training opportunities and utilizing a wide array of tools to help us work smarter, not harder. 

This book was created for you, dearest Virtual Assistant. This book is not a how-to meant to teach you to offer PR the way a full service firm would. **What is PR** 

*“If I was down to my last dollar, I’d spend it on public relations.”* – Bill Gates 

According to the Public Relations Society of America (PRSA), public relations is a “strategic communication process that builds mutually beneficial relationships between organizations and their publics.” 

Public relations is a practice which garners great publicity, or public awareness, for a product, service or company via the media. From a marketing perspective, publicity is one component of promotion and marketing. Other elements in the promotional mix are advertising, sales promotion, direct marketing and personal sales. 

It’s safe to say that every brand or entrepreneur could make use of public relations and benefit from a healthy dose of publicity. Every one of these business-minded folk needs to stay out in front of their prospects, engaging their customers on a regular basis in order to generate potential business. 

It doesn’t even matter what type of virtual assistant you might be. Whether you’re a generalist or you specialize in a niche industry, it’s safe to say your clientele will benefit from public relations. 

PR is like a cog in a bigger machine of integrated marketing and advertising strategy. It crosses all borders and is utilized worldwide by every tongue and nation. At the core of its driving force is a proactive searching for media coverage opportunities and potentialities for garnering favorable mentions.  
Many entrepreneurs and brands likely aren’t using PR as part of their current business strategy, but it’s certainly one that is equally beneficial to brands and companies of all sizes and industries. Each one, solopreneurs to small businesses and corporations, nonprofits and startups, authors, speakers – can all benefit from PR in their own way. Still, many entrepreneurs, nonprofits, etc. aren’t taking advantage of PR strategies. Why do you think this is? 

Hopefully we’re starting to get a little excited, imagining the prospects and possibilities when approaching our brands with a public relations mindset.  
**Why PR? Why Not Advertisement?** 

*“92% of consumers say they trust earned media, while only half trust paid ads.” –* Nielsen 

Nielsen conducted a recent Trust in Advertising Survey (TIA), identifying consumers’ three most trusted sources of information, in this order: 

1\. Recommendations from Friends and Family 

2\. Online Reviews 

3\. The Media 

People and businesses rely on third-party credibility to validate and vet companies and services before doing business with them, and these survey findings demonstrate that the media is a high ranking source in many consumers’ lives. 

Media coverage will offer depth and substance to your brand by: » Establishing third-party credibility   
» Gaining greater visibility 

» Achieving expert positioning 

» Garnering instant credibility 

» Attaining celebrity status 

» Receiving implied endorsements 

» Pre-selling your prospects 

The media technically doesn’t endorse your business, but it can often be perceived that way when they mention or feature your company or brand. If the media selects you or your business and not  
your competitor, will people assume you are special, or the best? To understand this further, let’s take a look at how public relations ranks in comparison to other types of media content. 

It’s helpful to look at all content as belonging to one of four different yet interconnected categories, or *PESO*. 

Paid *// Advertising, Paid Content Placement, Sponsored FB Posts* 

These examples hold the least amount of trust with consumers. After all, a company can, and sometimes does, say anything they want to about their business or product – expecting the public to take them at their word. 

Earned *// Media Mentions or Features* 

This content is of the highest value. Specifically selected for a write-up or feature. (Remember, this content avenue is top three in Nielsen’s advertising survey.) 

Shared *// Social Media, Social Engagement, Co-branding* This is valuable content that creates consumer interaction and social sharing. 

Owned *// Your websites, Blog posts, etc.* 

This type of content can create thought leadership. Managing content while pursuing alternative approaches to gain visibility and help encourage brand engagement. 

PR has consistently proven to be a powerful addition to an overall great marketing strategy – becoming ever more valuable once we shifted into “The Trust Economy.” Emerging from the use and development of sites like eBay (and later Airbnb) which invite us to do business with, and send money to, unknown sellers who’ve been deemed trustworthy by a few positive reviews.  
When was the last time you dined at a new restaurant without looking online at their reviews, checking for media coverage, or asking friends for their experiences? It is this trust (in the form of third-party validation) that rely on when deciding whether we will do business with a company or not. 

The media has become a top provider of this trust: a reliable source to readers and consumers everywhere.  
**Public Relations is Like the Lottery** 

Echoing the NY State lottery slogan, “You have to be in it to win it\!” 

Most of us are not going to be as lucky as Chris Pratt to be discovered by a talent agency while waiting tables at a Bubba Gump’s in Maui\! Occasionally, a product or brand will be discovered on a whim, but most companies will have to proactively pursue PR to gather any substantial amount of media mentions, coverage or features. Even still, many entrepreneurs, small businesses, nonprofits, etc. are not pursuing publicity or visibility for their brand. I believe there is still a bit of unnecessary mystique surrounding public relations. 

Here are a few common myths and misconceptions we can dispel: 

» PR is expensive 

» Only professionals or former journalists can understand PR strategy 

» If you want publicity, you have to hire a PR firm 

» You need solid connections 

» You must be a good writer 

» And so on…. 

When I speak to entrepreneurs, coaches, and small businesses that I’ve worked with, these are the Three Big Reasons many of them claim not to prioritize public relations: 

1\. Time  
2\. Money 

3\. Know-how 

Listen up “The Big Three” are a big reason I wrote this book\! I’ve spent a great amount of time thinking about how to make this process as easy as I can for anybody who’s looking to head up PR strategy for their brand or business. 

In your current role as Virtual Assistant, you can offer support services as an affordable alternative for entrepreneurs and companies that are interested in managing some, or all, of their own PR. (More about this soon.) As a VA, you are already helping people manage their time, freeing them up to focus on bigger projects and tasks as you take on greater and greater responsibility. And as a trained VA, you are already bringing a lot of know-how to your clients. 

In addition to any other training you may take to develop your knowledge of public relations, it is my hope, that after reading this book, you will be able to offer solid PR know-how to your clients.  
**Three Ways to Implement** 

*“Publicity is absolutely critical. A good PR story is infinitely more effective than a front-page ad.”* – Richard Branson 

There are a multitude of ways to implement a public relations campaign no matter the size of your business or your budget. PR can be spendy, but it doesn’t have to be. Certainly, hiring a firm to pursue PR strategies for your business can get expensive, but it’s not the only way. 

When I finally realized virtual assistants could solve many, if not all, of the obstacles preventing my clients from jumping into public relations, well, first I got excited. And then I got into action. 

The greatest challenge for entrepreneurs, coaches, consultants and businesses, even ones with a solid budget, is figuring out how to manage their PR strategy. There are three ways to begin implementing PR to the benefit of your brand. 

Most people think there are only two options: 

1\. Hire a PR firm 

2\. Do-It-Yourself (DIY) 

There is, however, a third option which is a hybrid method: 3\. DIY PR \+ Outsourcing   
This is where you manage the PR efforts yourself and outsource different aspects of your public relations initiatives to freelancers. (Many people don’t notice aspects of PR or tasks that can be easily outsourced.) It certainly doesn’t need to be an all-or-nothing  
proposition with the right team assembled. And a skilled virtual assistant can be the truest asset to any PR campaign.  
**The Three Methods: How Do They Compare** 

*“The caterpillar does all the work, but the butterfly gets all the publicity.” –* George Carlin 

*1\. The Traditional Approach: Hire a Firm* 

Benefits to this method: You will have experienced professionals leading your public relations campaign. You can mainly just sit back and relax as they handle your PR efforts for you. 

Hire the right firm, and this can be a great setup that allows you to focus more on your business and other tasks. Whichever firm you hire will easily be able to identify your best story hooks and the ways in which they can position you before the media to seem irresistible. 

A solid PR firm with existing relationships will be able to mine their network to collect media opportunities for you right out of the gate. 

The Cons: This method can be expensive. Potentially, you might get lost amongst the firm’s clients and not receive the individual attention you need and deserve. 

Mark Cuban, author and Shark Tank judge, believes that no one is as passionate about your company, product, or service as you are – which is why he believes you should explore other options before hiring a firm. 

*2\. The Do-It-Yourself Approach: DIY PR* 

Benefits: Savings in regard to the expense of having a PR firm on retainer, yet you will need to allocate abundant time and effort to implement your PR blueprint.  
To succeed at DIY PR, you will need to: 

» Learn how the media works 

» Come up with your brand’s ideal story hooks 

» Identify your target media contacts 

» Pitch and follow up those contacts 

DIY PR can quickly become a more successful method with additional training, coaching and mentoring. 

The Cons: PR can be a time-consuming undertaking. This can easily take you away from other work you want and need to be doing. You might not understand some of the nuances of the media, or you may be starting from Ground Zero where there is both a learning curve and ramp-up time. You likely won’t have access to the tools PR firms like to utilize, like personal contact lists and pricey subscription-based media databases. 

Yet, whether you are an entrepreneur, consultant or business owner, you can manage your brand’s public relations strategy and, indeed, have great success with it. 

Remember, nobody is more passionate about your brand’s mission than you are\! 

*3\. The Hybrid Approach: DIY PR \+ Outsourcing* 

The best of both worlds, the hybrid approach offers a way to maximize your time and your budget to get the publicity your brand needs at a reasonable resource cost. This method can help shorten your learning curve and allow you to outsource tasks that you may not be skilled at or feel comfortable doing.  
When using DIY PR with outsourcing, you are essentially acting as project manager over your brand’s PR blueprint, while finding ways to delegate additional tasks for implementation. 

What I like about this method is the ways you can maintain greater control over projects when deciding: 

» Which aspects you want to manage yourself 

» The amount of time you will be investing 

» What tasks you would prefer to outsource, and at what cost (market permitting) 

I believe this method can yield the best results because it combines your marketing skills and unique passion for your brand with that of a trained PR professional or Virtual Assistant. Additionally, this method can shorten the ramp-up time since your freelancer or VA will bring well-honed skills and assets along with them. 

The Cons: To be able to make solid hires, you need an understanding of PR, and know how to find and successfully manage freelancers or VA’s. Finding good PR freelancers can take time. You may want to try working with a few different freelancers before settling down with one. Hopefully when you find a great asset, you won’t need to hire again. 

Here is a list of PR skills you will need to develop (or outsource) when using the DIY PR method: 

» Media Kit Creation 

» Media List Creation 

» Online Media Room Creation 

» Creating or Identifying Story Hooks  
» Writing 

\- Press Release 

\- Pitch Letters 

\- Endorsement Requests 

\- Bylined Articles 

» Media Kit 

» Media Pitching and Follow-up 

» Monitoring and Pitching Media Queries 

Syms, a specialty New York City clothier, used to run an ad campaign that said: 

“An educated consumer is our best customer.” 

Whichever method you choose to use in pursuit of publicity – the more knowledge you seek to gain regarding public relations (how it works, which tools to use, etc.) the more fruitful your endeavors will be\!  
**Who Is (Are?) the Media** 

**“***If you don’t tell your story, someone else will.”* – Unknown 

Throughout a good portion of this book, I have mentioned a conglomeration known as “the media” without clearly defining what is being referred to. First, we will need to go back a little in time to provide some context for today’s media landscape. The term “media” previously referred to what was known as broadcast media: TV, radio, and print publications, including newspapers and magazines. 

There existed a strict distinction between paid and earned content during this time (ads versus mentions). Marketing and PR were very separate departments, even within a single company. Marketing teams would create marketing campaigns and were tasked with working with an ad agency to develop new programs. PR would work to develop relationships with journalists and secure media mentions and placements. 

The lines have blurred significantly from the days back when marketing departments and their ad agencies paid for distribution, yet PR never did. 

With the adoption of the internet, the definition of media began to expand as newspapers and magazines added online publications, and radio shows now produced podcasts. The advent of social media changed the definition forever. Every person and every company can now form a standalone media outlet. (Think: citizen journalist.) Anybody with an internet connection now has the ability to build and use a platform to share information and stories with unprecedented speed and consumer response.  
The growing importance of having Influencers in the media economy has created new opportunities for businesses and entrepreneurs to reach their target audiences. An influencer’s campaign or post can give these eager companies a powerful boost to help them reach the people they want to help most, while simultaneously garnering product interest and encouraging brand engagement. 

Let’s look at a real-world example. 

According to CNBC, Kylie Jenner receives one million dollars for every post she shares on Instagram. Let’s say Kylie posts a picture of herself wearing a pair of sunglasses and mentions the brand name in the caption. Her Instagram followers think these sunglasses must be her favorite. As a fashion trendsetter, she now influences/inspires her followers’ view of this brand – a positive view will undoubtedly lead to many sales. 

Essentially standing in as a paid spokesperson, who can really know if a celebrity actually prefers one product or another? Perhaps the influencer is simply saying what the brand asked them to say, the way traditional advertisements have done. 

Instead, businesses and consultants should strategically choose a star or celebrity to post or feature their product or service to intentionally develop the positive association between influencer and brand. 

Lines are blurred when influencers are paid to post on behalf of a brand, without mention of the arrangement being made public. All across the internet we are likely unaware of bloggers, hosts, tweets, and other content being promoted for profit without establishing trust or transparency.  
Instagram is now putting measures in place to raise awareness of brand/influencer relationships and paid posts. Account owners are now being asked to use the hashtags \#ad or \#sponsored. However, many influencers are using less obvious tags like \#sp (sponsored post), which followers may not recognize. 

Even segments on television stations that formerly operated as traditional media (with clear separation between paid and earned content) are now allowing brands and individuals to “pay to play” to be featured in a desired segment. This arrangement is not often disclosed to viewers. 

As I described earlier in the section laying out *PESO*, there is inherent value to each type of content. Intentionally utilizing each of them can help you develop your most effective PR strategy. 

A relatively recent shift has taken place in the media, where outlets are continuously on, day and night. This new format has created a continuous demand for fresh and interesting content. This creates awesome potential for brands and companies seeking opportunities for media coverage. 

Another shift we’ve seen happen in the media is the way magazines and online publications have opened up numerous opportunities for anybody to send a pitch or contribute content. 

Fresh additions to PR campaigns are collaborative projects such as guest blogging and contributed or bylined articles. Being written about in a publication like Forbes is very noteworthy. The cache of a top brand like Forbes is also transferred to an individual or company when they are featured as a contributor or guest blogger in that publication. Being mentioned or featured in the media has always been, and will always be, the gold standard.  
**The PR Process** 

*“It is always a risk to speak to the press: They are likely to report what you say.”* – Hubert H.Humphrey 

Let’s take a closer look at the process of PR strategy so you can better understand how you can personally offer PR support to your clients as a VA and learn what services you’ll be able to offer them. 

![][image3]  
***Identify Goals and Audience(s)*** 

To get started doing PR, a company needs to identify their goals and decide how to implement their PR blueprint. Earlier, I outlined three ways a company can handle their public relations. While developing goals and potential prospects, it would be a good time to decide which method of implementation the brand will go with (hiring a firm, doing it themselves, or using the hybrid method of outsourcing \+ DIY).  
Let’s talk first about identifying goals and strategies: 

It’s important for entrepreneurs and businesses to know what they want to get out of their PR campaigns. 

Is a company or consultant looking for more visibility and expert positioning? Is there a new target audience that a brand is trying to get in front of? Is a company launching a new product, service, book, or program? 

You may have heard the term customer avatar, a specific profile of a brand’s ideal prospect. It’s important to know who the avatar or avatars are for each of your client’s PR goals. Perhaps the company has a few dreams in mind – it’s important to understand exactly what the client wants to get out of their PR efforts, so they can effectively work towards achieving their goals. This step is a key aspect of successful PR. 

***Research*** 

Once the goals and avatars have been identified (whether this includes an existing customer profile or the development of entirely new ones), further research can be made into what media the avatar reads, watches and listens to. This is the process of building a targeted media list. 

Before moving full-steam ahead on creating a media list, it’s important to identify what type of media a company is seeking out. An entrepreneur who is camera shy or has a limited travel budget might exclude TV as a media target but include all the other types of outlets. 

Any media, or all media – from TV and print, to radio and online outlets, a media list will be most effective if it includes a combination of “dream” publications or shows. Entrepreneurs and companies  
often have a vision of their brand among specific, top national publications \[Ex: O Magazine\] or online TV programs \[Ex: The Today Show\]. 

The next level of research when creating a media list is identifying specific outlets. 

There are PR industry databases (paid) which can be used to build media lists (such as Cision or Muckrack). For individuals or smaller companies these services may be too expensive or overwhelming. Even if you use a media database to build a targeted list, I recommend researching each outlet personally, to insure accuracy of information and to educate yourself on the outlet and the specific contact. 

Once you have curated a list of targeted media outlets, it’s important to find the right contact at that outlet to communicate with, and eventually send your pitches to. In the case of a TV or radio show, the contact would be a producer or booker. For most print and online outlets, that contact would be a specific journalist. 

For an example, if you’re interested in being on a morning TV segment like Good Morning America or The Today Show, you would need to find the producer for that show or segment. If you’re looking to be featured or to become a contributor to Entrepreneur Magazine or another publication, you would need to find the name of the editor or particular journalist who covers your topic, so you can pitch properly. 

It’s important to make sure you identify the right journalists, producers, or bookers so you pitch someone who can actually write about your company or invite you onto their show.  
Editorial staff and journalists may change outlets, or even the topics they write about, so a media list needs to be maintained regularly. A lot of this information can be found on many publication websites, in the masthead, by doing some basic Google research, or by searching social media profiles. Some outlets and journalists are specific about how they like to be pitched – this sort of information is key, so add it to your media list and follow it closely when the time comes. 

***Media Preparation*** 

I call this part of media preparation, “getting ready for your close up\!” 

Of course, an author, coach, consultant or company will want to be ready for the media. While they already have access to stories and news, the development of media assets will make it easier for the media to vet brands and include them in stories. 

To be ready to meet the media, I recommend having the following handy: 

» Professional, high-resolution headshots 

» Biographies (both short and long) 

» Media Kit 

» Media Page (also referred to as an Online Media Room) 

Often, before writing about a person or company, the media will check them out online. The information in an online media room and press kit can offer enough background information to make a decision on whether the company or person is a fit for the story they are working on.  
Think of these media assets like automated PR assistants working for you non-stop. If a journalist is working on a story, burning the midnight oil before their morning deadline, and they need a source at 3 a.m., your business’ online media room and press kit can provide them with some or all of what they need to use. They meet their deadline and you get publicity – it’s a win-win situation. 

Additionally, it would be wise for your client to have their media assets ready before starting media outreach and pitching. If the media loves your pitch and wants to do a story, it is standard for them to ask for a photo and biography. For feature stories, they may send a photographer to create new images for the story. They may also rewrite your bio; however, they will want the current one for background information. 

*“PR happens when preparation meets opportunity.”* – Jane Tabachnick 

Another reason to be media-ready is professionality. While many online press rooms may be set up for the media, they are often perused by prospects who want to learn more about a company and the work that they do. A good media room provides social credibility to potential prospects, helping to presell them on a brand’s services and mission statement. 

***Implementation and Monitoring*** 

Now that goals are set, the media list is built, and the client is ready for their close up, we are ready for implementation. A PR campaign can be as simple as distributing a press release and posting on social media, or as comprehensive as an outreach campaign using email, phone and social media platforms.  
An important part of managing PR is monitoring news sites and social media for publicity and mentions. The media tries to let you know when they are going to run an article about you, to provide you with a live link or a copy, however, sometimes they are too busy and don’t tell you. It’s a pleasant surprise to find out you’ve gotten press or been mentioned\! And it’s something you will want to know about. 

It’s important to stay informed about what is being said about you and your brand, so you can leverage the conversation, engage it, and respond where necessary. When a person or company gets a media mention, it is also important to update their media room and media kit with fresh, key publicity. It is desirable to include it in your leverage and amplify strategy as well. (Read on to learn more about that.) Setting up tools and tasks to look out for media mentions is easy and will help streamline your monitoring efforts. There are many tools available to you, both free and paid. 

***Leverage and AmplifyTM*** 

You may have heard the adage, “If a tree falls in the forest…” 

If you want the most return on your investment from publicity, you’ll want to leverage and amplify it. When it comes to PR, I recommend you don’t assume that everyone, or anyone, has seen the press you’ve received – even if it was in the New York Times. Create a mini campaign to let people know about your press. Use your website, newsletter, social networks, etc. Publicity is the kind of content that you can repost on social media on a regular basis, extending the great benefits of media coverage to you again and again. 

Now that you have a greater awareness of how PR operates, I hope you can see all the opportunities around you for growth and service to both people and businesses. Entrepreneurs and  
companies, seeking your talents as a freelancer, will be tripping over their toes to land the competitive VA who might just jump start the PR department\!  
**Size Matters** 

*“It’s not the size of the dreamer, it’s the size of the dream.”* – Josh Ryan Evans 

Larger corporations often have in-house PR departments or firms on retainer. There are still opportunities with these larger organizations, however, they may only bring you on when they have a large initiative they’re working on, or a new product to launch. Circumstances such as rapid growth within the company or being short-staffed due to hiring changes – all these situations create potential opportunities for you. The opportunities may be short-term, but they can still be rewarding. 

Medium-sized companies might be set up like the corporations previously mentioned, or they can have a less-robust PR solution. In some cases, PR is folded in as part of their marketing department. These midsize companies may have more ongoing needs for a skilled PR VA to help them with their public relations initiatives. They may also have short-term needs from time to time. 

Smaller businesses and entrepreneurs, coaches, and consultants may not have a dedicated PR team or even conduct ongoing PR, or any public relations at all. They may implement public relations as needed only – when they launch a new product or have some other noteworthy event. 

By offering a variety of options, from project-based PR to ongoing support, you can make it possible for the solopreneur, entrepreneur, coach, or consultant, to build a consistent public relations initiative, and thereby reap publicity.  
These smaller clients are ideal prospects for PR VA’s, as they lack the time and resources to implement a solid PR strategy on an ongoing basis – even if they would like to\! They’re likely doing their best to manage their PR efforts alone. However, when they finally decide to outsource some of their tasks to a trained PR VA (that’s you\!), you can take the gems I’ve delivered in this guide and cultivate a smooth-running PR campaign that interests your client’s customers and reaches the hearts of their prospective masses.

For startup companies who are still in the idea phase, and established companies, non-profits, and solopreneurs alike – a PR blueprint can supply them with promising benefits and bountiful rewards. 

In every industry, in every country around the globe, everyone could use a little publicity.

**Glossary** 

**Breaking News** 

Newly received information about an event that is currently occurring or developing. It is a current issue that broadcasters feel warrants the interruption of scheduled programming and/or current **news** in order to report its details1. 

Ex \- a plane crash 

Also called: late breaking news, a special report, special coverage or **news** bulletin 

**Electronic Press Kit \[EPK\]** 

An electronic press kit (EPK) is a press kit equivalent in electronic form. An EPK usually takes the form of a website or e-mailable digital file \[PDF\], though they are also known to exist in CD and DVD form EPK. They are popular with artists and musicians, as they offer an easy way to share audio clips, tour dates, etc.1 

Also called \- press kit, media kit 

**Influencer** 

Individuals who have the power to affect purchase decisions of others because of their (real or perceived) authority, knowledge, position, or relationship. In consumer spending, members of a peer group or reference group act as influencers. In business to business (organizational) buying, internal employees (engineers, managers, purchasers) or external consultants act as influencers.2Instagram influencers – a celebrity or person with a large following – are often hired by brands to promote products via paid posts. 

**Masthead**  
A statement printed in all issues of a newspaper, magazine, or the like, usually on the editorial page, giving the publication’s name, the names of the owner and staff, etc.8 

**Media List** 

A list that documents the key media contacts who would be interested in stories about your business or area of expertise. These media contacts may include journalists, reporters, bloggers, producers, freelance writers and editors across print, online, blogs, podcasts, radio and television. 

**Media Outlet** 

A publication or broadcast program that provides news and feature stories to the public through various distribution channels. Media outlets include newspapers, magazines, radio, television, and the Internet3, and can also include podcasts and other media… 

Also called \- the media 

**Media relations** 

Working with the media for the purpose of informing the public of an organization’s mission, policies and practices in a positive, consistent and credible manner. Typically, this means coordinating directly with the people responsible for producing the news and features in the mass media.1 Media relations refers to the mutually beneficial relationship between journalists and public relations professionals. 

**Media Monitoring** 

The process of reading, watching or listening to the editorial content of media sources and social media on a continuing basis to find out when you have press mentions, or when specific keywords, topics or competitors get mentioned. 

**Mention**  
An instance of citing or calling attention to someone or something.4 On social media, mentions have come to mean specific utterances of a user’s social profile. 

**News Wire** 

A news agency or organization that supplies new stories to newspapers, radio, and television stations. Formerly transmitted via a wire, the news is now distributed \[syndicated\] via RSS technology. 

Also called: Wire Service 

**One Sheet** 

A one page ‘media kit’ featuring highlights from your complete media kit. Often used to pitch radio or podcast hosts, event planners etc. It is also used by bloggers and podcast hosts to provide information to potential advertisers, who include viewership and engagement statistics. 

Also called: One Sheet Media Kit, One Sheet Press Kit, Author One Sheet, Speaker One Sheet 

**Newsjacking** 

The process of injecting your brand into the day’s news, creating a twist that grabs eyes when they’re open widest.5 The practice of taking advantage of current events or news stories in such a way as to promote or advertise one’s product or brand.6 

**Online Media Room** 

A website, web page or site section that contains distributable information about a corporation or organization. This page can include news releases, PR contact info, press kit, etc. It is often geared to make it easier for the media to write about you but is also used to showcase media coverage to add credibility for prospects to learn more about a brand.  
Also called: Press Room, Media Page, Press Page, Online Newsroom 

**Press Kit** 

A folio or pre-packaged set of promotional materials that provide information about a person, company, organization, product or cause and which is available online or distributed to members of the media to provide key information for promotional use. 

The best press kits make it easy for reporters to quickly learn about the product and brand, and access photos and marketing materials they can use. 

For bloggers or podcast hosts, the press kit is sometimes geared for advertisers, in which case it would offer traffic stats, downloads etc. to provide social proof, viewership and engagement information. 

Also called: A Media Kit 

**Press Release** 

A written, or recorded communication or official statement directed at members of the news media for the purpose of announcing something ostensibly newsworthy or giving information on a particular matter. 

Also called: news release, media release, press statement or video release 

**Press Release Distribution** 

The process of distributing your press release out to the media. You can use a service \[newswire\] that will send your release out to various outlets like newspapers, magazines and the like, or you can post your release to press release distribution websites \[journalists my search these sites for keywords or topics\]. You can send your  
press release to a targeted list of journalists and media outlets who cover your topic 

**Public Relations \[PR\]** 

A strategic communication process that builds mutually beneficial relationships between organizations and their publics.7It is the professional maintenance of a favorable public image by a company or other organization or a famous person.8 

**Publicity** 

The notice or attention given to someone or something by the media. Publicity is gaining public visibility or awareness for a product, service or your company via the media. From a marketing perspective, publicity is one component of promotion and marketing. The other elements of the promotional mix are advertising, sales promotion, direct marketing and personal selling.1
